paper_title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress in complex reasoning, driven in part by increasingly capable pretrained models and post-training on ever-larger reasoning corpora (Wei et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2025). prevailing line of work is to scale supervision with more reasoning trajectories to train on (Zelikman et al., 2022b; GLM-5-Team et al., 2026). However, this scaling incurs substantial training cost without proportional performance gains, motivating shift from simply increasing data volume toward identifying reasoning trajectories with greater learning value He et al. (2026); Hou et al. (2026). Existing efforts broadly explore two complementary directions: constructing more effective reasoning supervision through stronger teacher generation and trajectory augmentation (Guo et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023), and improving the utilization of fixed corpora through filtering or routing based on correctness (Slinko et al., 2026; Guha et al., 2025), difficulty (Tian et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026), or quality (Li et al., 2026; Just et al., 2026). While achieving promising results, neither direction is sufficient for extreme optimization efficiency. As result, achieving such efficiency requires coupling supervision construction with downstream allocation: first exposing where learning value resides, and then progressively concentrating optimization on it. 1 Published as conference paper at ICLR 2027 Figure 1: Correct and confident CoTs can still conceal fragile reasoning. Left: Even among the top-5% teacher-confident CoTs, 18.1% fall within the global top-10% uncertainty tail. Mid: Likewise, 30.5% of correct CoTs fall within the same uncertainty tail. Right: Motivated by this, we propose an uncertaintyguided progressive contraction framework. By progressively narrowing supervision from uncertaintyinformative teacher reasoning to learner-relevant trajectories, we achieve competitive reasoning performance with 18.7 fewer post-training steps. To expose learning-critical information, we exploit the internal structure of reasoning. In fact, reasoning is inherently non-uniform: solution often hinges on small number of intermediate states where plausible continuations diverge toward different outcomes, which we term reasoning forks. Such forks naturally manifest as process-level uncertainty, as alternative continuations from the same reasoning state may lead to both successful and unsuccessful solutions. As shown in Fig. 1, even highly confident or correct Chain of Thoughts (CoTs) can conceal substantial process-level uncertainty, suggesting that terminal confidence and correctness may mask fragile intermediate reasoning (Zelikman et al., 2022a; Zhao, 2026; Mao et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2025b). Consistent with prior work showing that uncertainty reveals local failures and reasoning boundary (Kadavath et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026c; Mei et al., 2025), we therefore view process uncertainty as behavioral signature of the reasoning capability boundary. Motivated by this, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework for efficient reasoning post-training. We first construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision trajectories by building Monte Carlo Reasoning Trees (MCRTs) around intermediate states and estimating correct-answer reachability and branch-outcome uncertainty from sampled continuations. Aggregated process uncertainty contracts the original corpus into compact teacher-informed candidate pool along with uncertainty profiles. During student SFT, however, the uncertainty-profiled CoTs remain learner-agnostic and do not reflect the students evolving training state. Thus, we introduce second learner-aware contraction, which narrows the candidate set by routing optimization according to the students evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively concentrate supervision from teacher-informative to learner-relevant trajectories, reducing both data usage and, more importantly, the optimization required to learn from it. As result, our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450 less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Experimental results across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM architectures demonstrate that our method substantially accelerates SFT training while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Our framework presents strong cross-student transferability: reasoning supervision distilled from the same Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025a) teacher generalizes effectively across heterogeneous student families, including Qwen3.5-4B/9B (Qwen Team, 2026), Gemma-4 E4B (Team et al., 2026), Llama-3.2-3BInstruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Mistral-7B-Instruct (Jiang et al., 2023). Importantly, the gains extend beyond efficiency: our 9B student achieves competitive reasoning performance with substantially larger reasoning models ranging from 30B to 671B parameters. Notably, because uncertainty is characterized purely through observable reasoning behavior, the same framework applies to API-only black-box teachers (e.g., DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) and Kimi-K2.6 (Moonshot AI, 2026)) and teachers substantially smaller than their students. For instance, Qwen3-1.7B teacher can improve much stronger Qwen3.5-14B student, demonstrating effective reasoning transfer. 2 Published as conference paper at ICLR 2027 Our main contributions are as follows: (1) We introduce an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework for data-efficient reasoning post-training, jointly integrating supervision construction and downstream training allocation to progressively concentrate learning on high-value reasoning trajectories. (2) We introduce uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision, modeling MCRTs to expose process-level reasoning forks from observable model behavior without requiring model-internal access. (3) We develop learneraware routing that further contracts the active training set during SFT according to the students evolving learning state, enabling enhanced training acceleration. (4) Across diverse benchmarks, model families, and teacher regimes, our method reduces reasoning optimization to as little as < 0.74%, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance, establishing practical pathway toward data-efficient reasoning post-training for future research.

sections.content: Uncertainty-Guided Data-Efficient Training. As shown in Table 1, we evaluate reasoning distillation across competition mathematics, general mathematics, and scientific reasoning, using Qwen3-8B as common teacher and Qwen3.5-4B/9B as students on DAPO-17k . It can be seen that progressive contraction yields substantial reductions in both training budget and practical training costs while preserving or improving reasoning performance. Across Qwen3.5-4B and 9B students, our method uses only 0.221.91% of the full-SFT optimization budget, reducing SFT time from 8.47/9.23 hours to only 0.010.07 hours. Under ρ = 1%, our method brings over 800 wall-clock acceleration, yet the resulting models remain competitive with or outperform full-set SFT across most benchmarks. Importantly, this efficiency persists as the student scales from 4B to 9B, highlighting its generality. Moreover, performance remains remarkably stable under increasingly aggressive contraction, demonstrating that our progressive contraction effectively concentrates optimization on high-value supervision. three Cross-Family Student Generalization. We next examine whether the optimization efficiency generalizes across student distinct model families. Using the same Qwen3-8B teacher, we evaluate heterogeneous students: Gemma-4-E4B-IT, LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct, covering different of reasoning capability. As shown in Fig. 2, our method maintains or improves overall reasoning performance across all three student families while using only approximately 0.45% of the full-SFT student-side optimization budget, corresponding to over 200 training acceleration. The consistent effectiveness under such aggressive contraction demonstrates that the efficiency gains are not specific to particular student architecture. Importantly, once the teacher-side uncertainty profile is constructed from the same Qwen3-8B teacher, it can be shared across students, highlighting strong cross-family transfer and effectiveness. To better understand the efficiency of our method, as shown in Figure 1, we track the optimization trajectories and compare them with the full SFT. It shows that our method surpasses the full SFT within only 150 steps, whereas full SFT requires about 1500 steps to reach its optimum, corresponding to 10 fewer optimization steps. Teacher Uncertainty and Learner Routing Are Complementary. We ablate both stages of progressive contraction. As shown in Table 6, each component improves accuracy, while their combination yields the best performance. Importantly, both stages contribute along complementary axes: the former improves the informativeness of the candidate supervision space, while learner-aware routing concentrates SFT updates on trajectories with greater student-specific learning demand. The substantially larger gain from their combination supports the central design of progressive contraction: first preserve informative reasoning supervision, and then allocate optimization according to training dynamics.

sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Uncertainty in LLM Reasoning and Learning. Uncertainty quantification has been studied as means of characterizing the reliability and knowledge boundaries of LLMs (Shorinwa et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025a). Existing approaches estimate uncertainty through token probabilities, verbalized confidence, sampling-based disagreement, and semantic entropy (Manakul et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2026). Recent studies further show that stronger or longer reasoning does not necessarily yield better uncertainty awareness, with modern reasoning models often remaining overconfident or increasingly miscalibrated on incorrect predictions (Mei et al., 2025; Yeom et al., 2026). Beyond final-answer confidence, process-level uncertainty has been modeled over intermediate reasoning states through Monte Carlo continuation, confidence probing, and calibration-aware supervision (Wang et al., 2026b; Park et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026). For instance, RLCM (Wang et al., 2026a) introduces confidence-aware process supervision and improves calibration while preserving reasoning accuracy. These works motivate treating uncertainty as structured signal of reasoning stability and capability boundaries throughout multi-step reasoning. (Wang et al., 2026b; Park et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026). Data-Efficient Distillation and Adaptive Data Routing. Knowledge distillation provides data-centric mechanism for transferring capabilities from stronger teachers to smaller learners (Hsieh et al., 2023; Shridhar et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026d). For reasoning tasks, recent work increasingly distills intermediate rationales or long-form CoTs rather than final answers alone, enabling students to acquire richer reasoning behaviors (Liu et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026a;b). Beyond increasing the amount of reasoning supervision, growing evidence suggests that its effectiveness depends strongly on trajectory form and learner compatibility (Yang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026b). Accordingly, reasoning supervision has been adapted through trajectory filtering (Yang et al., 2026b), prefix alignment (Liu et al., 2026), difficulty-aware supervision (Wu et al., 2026a), and student-conditioned trajectory selection (Zhang et al., 2026a; He et al., 2026). In parallel, data selection and valuation methods allocate training computation toward more useful examples (Yang et al., 2025b; Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020), using signals such as quality (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025c), diversity (Zheng et al., 2023), gradient or influence information (Yang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2026c), and model-dependent learning dynamics (Engstrom et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Representative approaches include DEITA (Liu et al., 2024), LESS (Xia et al., 2024), Data Agent (Yang et al., 2026a), and RHO-Loss (Mindermann et al., 2022). These methods can be broadly viewed as data routing: allocating limited optimization toward supervision with greater expected learning value.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that exposes and concentrates learning value in reasoning supervision, substantially accelerating reasoning post-training without sacrificing capability. Across diverse benchmarks and architectures, our method consistently improves data efficiency with strong generalization. These results highlight that effective reasoning supervision depends not only on scale, but also on how learning value is identified and allocated throughout training. More broadly, we hope this work inspires further research on the shift from scaling reasoning data toward more efficient and accessible reasoning post-training, while providing practical tool to reduce training burden and enable strong reasoning models under limited computational resources for the community. 9 Published as conference paper at ICLR
